opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference is in the linear attention module itself. MiniMax M1 used Lightning Attention, which is essentially a fairly vanilla linear attention, with no real decay or gating mechanism. It was hybridized with softmax attention, roughly seven linear layers to one full attention layer, and they showed you can scale that to a very large model. That was an important existence proof. But the linear part was relatively weak in expressiveness. Without forgetting, the state keeps accumulating everything, and its retrieval and in-context recall ability is limited.

What Kimi did with Kimi Linear builds on the delta rule line of work, things like DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. The delta rule gives you something like an online learning update. Instead of just adding key-value outer products into the state, you correct the state toward the new association, so it behaves much more like an associative memory that can overwrite stale information. Kimi Delta Attention adds a finer-grained gate on top of that, channel-wise decay rather than a single scalar per head. That gives the model more control over what to forget in each dimension of the memory.

The other important part is engineering. A finer-grained gate is only useful if you can train it efficiently. A lot of the work went into making the chunkwise parallel algorithm hardware-friendly, so that it stays efficient on GPUs and doesn't become a bottleneck compared with simpler linear attention.

So I'd say the improvement is threefold. First, a much more expressive recurrent update. Second, better gating. Third, careful kernel design so that this expressiveness doesn't cost you throughput. Together, that lets the hybrid model match or beat full attention on quality rather than just being cheaper. That's the shift I find most exciting. Linear attention moves from "an efficient approximation" to "a genuinely competitive architecture choice."

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is actually in how the two teams framed the problem, rather than any single architectural trick.

MiniMax M1 at the start of the year was, in a sense, a proof of existence. They showed that you could take a hybrid design, with lightning attention interleaved with a small fraction of full softmax attention layers, scale it to a very large MoE, and get a model that was competitive on long-context reasoning while being much cheaper at inference. That was important. Before M1, a lot of people in the industry still had the attitude that linear attention is a nice academic toy, but nobody serious would bet a frontier model on it. M1 broke that psychological barrier.

But if you look closely, the linear part of M1 is fairly simple. Lightning attention is essentially a linear attention with a fixed decay, no data-dependent gating, no delta rule. The recurrent state is updated in a very plain way. So the model leans quite heavily on the softmax layers to do the hard retrieval work, and the linear layers mostly provide cheap, local context. The ablations they reported were also relatively thin, so it was hard to tell from the outside how much of the quality came from the hybrid design versus from scale and RL.

What Kimi did with Kimi Linear is, to me, more interesting from a modeling perspective. The core layer, KDA, is a gated delta rule variant with fine-grained, per-channel gating. So instead of one scalar decay for the whole state, each dimension of the recurrent state can forget at its own rate, and the delta rule lets the model actively overwrite stale associations rather than just letting them decay. That matters a lot for things like in-context retrieval and for long-horizon reasoning where you need to keep some information sharp and discard other information quickly.

The second thing is the hybrid ratio and the design of the full-attention layers. Kimi used a 3:1 ratio of KDA to full attention and used MLA for the global layers, and crucially they dropped the position encoding in the global layers. That is a nice detail. The linear layers already carry positional information through the recurrence, so the softmax layers can be truly content-based, which helps length extrapolation. M1 did not go that far.

The third thing, and honestly the one I care about most, is that Kimi did the controlled experiments properly. They trained the same architectures on the same data at the same scale and compared against a strong MLA baseline and against GDN-H, so you can actually see that the gains come from the layer design and not just from a different training recipe. In our community that kind of fair comparison is rare, and it makes the result much more trustworthy.

And then the engineering side: the chunkwise kernel for KDA is well optimized, it is integrated into FLA, and the vLLM support was there at release. So the efficiency claims are not just theoretical; you can measure the decoding throughput gain at one million tokens yourself.

So to summarize, M1 showed that hybrid linear attention could work at frontier scale, and Kimi showed that if you take the linear layer seriously, with proper gating, a delta rule, and a carefully designed hybrid, you can actually beat full attention at equal compute rather than just match it at lower cost. That is a meaningful shift in the argument.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate improvements in the model itself from improvements in how the work was demonstrated. For the model, I’d look at whether it can carry a difficult task through to completion—especially when that involves multiple steps or tools—rather than just produce a strong answer to an isolated question. For the demonstration, I’d ask whether the results make those gains clear and reproducible.

But I wouldn’t confidently attribute a specific improvement to Kimi over MiniMax M1 without pinning down which Kimi release and which results we’re comparing. Are you thinking about the architecture, the training approach, or the practical performance?

r001.rationale: The response discusses model capability generally but does not identify a linear-attention module as Kimi’s main improvement.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Lightning Attention or characterize it as being at the RetNet stage.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute stronger linear attention to recent advances in linear-attention methods.

r004.rationale: It does not compare Kimi’s and MiniMax M1’s MoE granularity.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: did the underlying model get better, and did it become more useful as an agent? Those aren’t quite the same thing. A model can improve on reasoning benchmarks without getting much better at completing a task that involves tools, several steps, and recovering from mistakes.

That’s the lens I’d use to compare Kimi with MiniMax M1: how reliably does it carry a task through to completion, and at what cost? I’d want a side-by-side comparison before attributing the difference to a particular training or architecture choice. Otherwise, it’s easy to mistake a better overall system for a breakthrough in one specific component.
